concepts.title: Area Under a Curve as a Definite Integral
concepts.definition: The region trapped between a curve, the x-axis and two vertical lines is filled with thin rectangles of height y and width dx; adding their areas turns the question into one definite integral of the function between the two vertical lines.
concepts.formula: area = integral from lower to upper of f(x) dx
concepts.key_idea: Thin vertical strips convert a planar region into a single definite integral.

solution_steps.action: Read off the bounding curve and the two vertical boundaries
solution_steps.explain: The ordinates become the lower and upper limits of integration.

solution_steps.action: Write the strip element of height y and width dx
solution_steps.explain: Each thin rectangle contributes y dx, so the total is the integral of y dx.

solution_steps.action: Evaluate the definite integral of the curve between the limits
solution_steps.explain: The antiderivative difference gives the geometric area.

concepts.title: Area Using Horizontal Strips with x as a Function of y
concepts.definition: When the boundary is easier to describe sideways, horizontal strips of width dy are used instead: the region against the y-axis between two horizontal lines integrates the x-expression over that y-interval.
concepts.formula: area = integral from c to d of g(y) dy where the curve is x = g(y)
concepts.key_idea: Swap the roles of the axes: integrate x over y to sweep horizontal strips.
concepts.textbook_ref: lemh202.txt section 8.2 horizontal strips (lines ~68-100) and example 1 alternative

solution_steps.action: Rewrite the boundary equation with x alone on one side
solution_steps.explain: Solving for x in terms of y gives the strip length g(y).

solution_steps.action: Identify the y-values of the horizontal boundaries
solution_steps.explain: These become the limits c and d of the dy integral.

solution_steps.action: Integrate g(y) dy between the limits
solution_steps.explain: The sweep of horizontal rectangles equals the region area.

concepts.title: Area When Parts of the Curve Lie Below the Axis
concepts.definition: A definite integral signed by the axis gives negative contributions where the curve dips under; geometric area is recovered by splitting the interval at every axis crossing and adding the absolute value of each piece.
concepts.formula: total_area = absolute value of piece1 + absolute value of piece2 over the split intervals
concepts.key_idea: Split at the zeros of the curve, then add magnitudes instead of signed values.
question_patterns: find the true area when the curve goes below the x axis

solution_steps.action: Locate the zeros of the curve inside the interval
solution_steps.explain: Each crossing divides the region into an above-axis and a below-axis part.

solution_steps.action: Integrate separately over each sub-interval
solution_steps.explain: Sub-integrals inherit the sign of the curve on that stretch.

solution_steps.action: Add the absolute values of the sub-integrals
solution_steps.explain: Geometric area is never negative, so magnitudes are summed.

concepts.title: Area Enclosed by a Circle by Integration
concepts.definition: For the circle of radius r centred at the origin, the upper half has height the square root of r squared minus x squared; symmetry lets one integrate over the first quadrant and multiply by four, which reproduces the familiar pi r squared.
concepts.formula: area of the circle = pi * radius**2
concepts.key_idea: Integrate one quadrant of the circle and multiply by four by symmetry.
question_patterns: find the area enclosed by the circle using integration

solution_steps.action: Compute one quadrant of the disc
solution_steps.explain: Symmetry makes the quadrant exactly a quarter of the full circle.

solution_steps.action: Multiply the quadrant by four
solution_steps.explain: The four symmetric quarters assemble the whole circle.

concepts.title: Area Enclosed by an Ellipse by Integration
concepts.definition: For the standard ellipse with semi-axes a and b, the upper branch has height b over a times the square root of a squared minus x squared; integrating one quadrant and multiplying by four yields pi times the product of the semi-axes.
concepts.formula: area of the ellipse = pi * axis_a * axis_b
concepts.key_idea: One quadrant of the ellipse integrates to pi times a times b over four.
question_patterns: find the area of the region bounded by the ellipse with given semi axes

solution_steps.action: Compute one quadrant of the elliptical region
solution_steps.explain: Symmetry gives a quarter of the whole ellipse.

solution_steps.action: Multiply the quadrant by four
solution_steps.explain: Assembling the four quadrants covers the full ellipse.

concepts.title: Area Between a Line and the x-axis Between Two Ordinates
concepts.definition: For a straight line sitting wholly above the x-axis on an interval, the swept region is a trapezium whose signed integral equals the antiderivative of the line at the right ordinate minus its value at the left ordinate.
concepts.formula: area under the line = integral from lower to upper of slope*x + intercept dx
concepts.key_idea: A line's area is the antiderivative difference across the two ordinates.
question_patterns: find the area bounded by the line and the x axis between two ordinates
compute the trapezium area under a straight line by integration
evaluate the region swept under the line from the left ordinate to the right ordinate

solution_steps.action: Antiderivative of the line at the right ordinate
solution_steps.explain: The primitive of slope*x + intercept is slope*x**2/2 + intercept*x.

solution_steps.action: Antiderivative of the line at the left ordinate
solution_steps.explain: The same primitive is evaluated at the lower limit.

solution_steps.action: Subtract to sweep out the area
solution_steps.explain: The difference of the two values equals the bounded area.

concepts.title: Area Under a Power Curve Between Two Limits
concepts.definition: For a power curve y equals a constant times x to the exponent, the region above the axis integrates by the power rule: lift the exponent by one, divide, then subtract the antiderivative values at the two limits.
concepts.formula: area under the power curve = coef * (upper**(exp1 + 1) - lower**(exp1 + 1)) / (exp1 + 1)
concepts.key_idea: The power rule plus a limit subtraction measures the region under a power curve.
question_patterns: find the area under the curve y equals x squared between two x values

solution_steps.action: Apply the power rule at the upper limit
solution_steps.explain: The primitive coef*x**(exp1+1)/(exp1+1) is evaluated at upper.

solution_steps.action: Apply the power rule at the lower limit
solution_steps.explain: The same primitive is evaluated at lower.

solution_steps.action: Subtract the two values
solution_steps.explain: Upper minus lower is the area of the region.

concepts.title: Symmetry Shortcuts for Standard Curves
concepts.definition: Closed standard curves centred on the axes are symmetric in both directions, so the full enclosed area equals four times the first-quadrant part; this avoids integrating over the whole figure.
concepts.formula: total enclosed area = 4 * integral from 0 to a of y dx over the first quadrant branch
concepts.key_idea: Compute one symmetric piece and scale up instead of integrating everywhere.

solution_steps.action: Check the curve for reflection symmetry in both axes
solution_steps.explain: Standard centred circles and ellipses mirror across the x and y axes.

solution_steps.action: Set up the integral over the first quadrant branch only
solution_steps.explain: The quadrant piece carries positive y throughout.

solution_steps.action: Multiply the quadrant area by four
solution_steps.explain: The four mirrored copies tile the whole enclosed region.
